Family Health

Sexual health for men: consent, communication and care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Sexual wellbeing involves physical health, personal preferences and the freely expressed wishes of anyone you are intimate with. There is no single script for how a man should behave or what a successful encounter must achieve. Honest communication and appropriate medical care can make room for comfort, choice and changing needs.

Support general health without promising a performance result

Regular activity, suitable food, enough rest and help with stress can support overall and sexual health. Smoking, heavy drinking and some recreational drugs can contribute to erection problems. Changes are worth discussing even when sexual symptoms are not the only concern.

These habits do not guarantee confidence, desire or a particular response. Fatigue, illness, relationship circumstances and medicines also matter. A difficulty is not evidence of poor character or insufficient effort, and needing treatment does not mean a healthy lifestyle has failed.

Accept a refusal as an answer

If a partner says no, accept it. A quick refusal does not mean you chose the wrong words and should try a more persuasive approach. Consent must be freely given, specific to the activity and open to being withdrawn.

Previous sex, a relationship, affection or a physical response does not create permission. When someone is unsure, quiet, uncomfortable or no longer participating, stop and check. A person who cannot freely choose or communicate agreement cannot give consent. Neither partner owes an explanation before an activity stops.

Let affection and preparation be a shared choice

People differ in whether they want touch, closeness or sexual activity at a particular time. What is often called foreplay should be a mutually wanted part of intimacy, not a strategy for changing a refusal into agreement. Someone may want affection without wanting intercourse.

Discuss preferences and limits at a calm moment rather than relying on a scene from a film or an assumption about gender. Saying what feels comfortable, what you would prefer and what you do not want can be useful. No list of techniques can replace listening to the person with you.

Masturbation is not automatically a relationship problem

Some people masturbate while in a relationship and others do not. It can feel relaxing or pleasurable, but it is not a duty or a treatment everyone needs. Private sexual behaviour does not by itself prove dissatisfaction with a partner.

Couples may discuss privacy and boundaries without turning the conversation into an inspection of each other. If either person wants to share or discuss an intimate activity, both must freely agree. Watching a partner or disclosing personal preferences is optional, not a required way to learn about each other.

Separate masturbation myths from symptoms that need help

Masturbation does not ordinarily cause erectile dysfunction or permanently weaken an erection. Friction or rough handling can nevertheless cause sore skin or injury. Stop when there is pain, swelling or bleeding and seek care when symptoms are significant or persist.

There is no universal number that defines too much. Consider whether the behaviour feels hard to control, causes injury, interferes with sleep, work or other responsibilities, or creates distress. A sexual-health professional or therapist can help assess the pattern without making shame the treatment.

Avoid turning intimacy into an exchange or an exam

Giving attention or participating in one activity does not entitle anyone to a return favour. Discussing mutual satisfaction is different from demanding gratitude, a particular sound or an orgasm. A person may express enjoyment quietly and should not need to perform it for reassurance.

An unhurried setting and fewer phone or television distractions may help connection when both people want that. Being attentive to the person with you matters more than rigid rules about words or behaviour. It is always acceptable to pause for discomfort, an interruption or a change of mind rather than prioritise a planned outcome.

Discuss boundaries before changing the activity

Do not introduce rough contact or a more intense activity on the assumption that a partner will object if it is unwanted. Agreeing to one kind of contact does not authorise another. Pain should prompt a stop and a check, not an expectation that someone must endure it.

A prearranged signal can be useful, but nobody has to remember a special word for their boundary to count. An ordinary request to stop, withdrawing or uncertainty is enough to pause. Consent is not made permanent by a conversation earlier in the day.

Include infection and pregnancy prevention

Many sexually transmitted infections have no obvious symptoms. Talk about appropriate testing and which body sites it covers, rather than treating a symptom-free appearance or one past result as a guarantee. Condoms and other barriers reduce several risks but do not prevent every infection involving uncovered skin.

Ask about HPV and hepatitis B vaccination and HIV prevention when relevant to your exposure. If pregnancy is possible and not wanted, discuss a contraceptive plan too. A method that prevents pregnancy may provide no protection against an infection. Both people should understand the plan and be able to revisit it.

Understand what erectile dysfunction describes

Erectile dysfunction means difficulty getting or maintaining an erection sufficient for the sexual activity wanted. Occasional difficulties can happen with stress, tiredness or alcohol. Repeated difficulties may involve blood flow, nerves, diabetes, hormone problems, medicine effects or psychological factors, often in combination.

It becomes more common with age, but age does not make assessment pointless. A fixed percentage for every decade cannot describe an individual. Erection difficulties do not automatically mean lack of attraction, low testosterone or a purely psychological problem.

Use assessment to identify the relevant causes

A clinician may ask about when the problem occurs, other erections, desire, pain, medical history, medicines and relationship stress. Blood pressure and selected checks for diabetes, cholesterol or hormones may be useful. An examination or specialist referral depends on the findings.

Bring a list of prescription medicines, over-the-counter products and recreational substances. Do not stop treatment yourself because you suspect a sexual side effect; a safer dose or alternative may be available. Counselling or psychosexual therapy can accompany physical treatment, and partner involvement should be your choice.

Erection medicines require an individual safety check

Sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil are examples of PDE5 inhibitors, which support blood flow involved in an erection. They are not interchangeable with testosterone or guaranteed to solve every cause. Timing, interactions and suitability depend on the medicine and your health.

Do not combine these medicines with nitrate treatment for chest pain or recreational nitrites such as poppers; the blood-pressure drop can be dangerous. Tell the prescriber about heart or liver disease and all other products. Use an appropriately regulated prescribing or pharmacy service rather than an unidentified online performance product.

Testosterone is for a confirmed deficiency, not routine enhancement

Testosterone treatment may be considered when compatible symptoms occur with consistently low measured levels and an appropriate assessment. A clinician usually confirms the result with repeat morning testing and investigates the cause. A single low value or erection difficulty alone is not enough.

Gel, patches and injections are among possible forms, depending on local availability and circumstances. They need follow-up for benefit and adverse effects. Tell the clinician about future pregnancy plans before treatment: testosterone supplied from outside the body can suppress sperm production and is not a fertility treatment.

Know how injections, vacuum devices and implants differ

Specialist medicines can be injected into the penis or, for some products, placed in the urethra. They require a prescription, individual instruction and a plan for adverse effects. They are not automatically safe for every person who cannot take a tablet, and this is not a procedure to learn from a general article.

An external vacuum device uses a cylinder and pump to draw blood into the penis, often with a ring to maintain the erection. A penile prosthesis is different: it is implanted surgically and may be inflatable or a bendable device. Most people do not need surgery; discuss alternatives, practical use, complications and long-term expectations with a urologist.

Recognise urgent problems and keep follow-up open

An erection lasting more than four hours needs emergency assessment, especially after an erection medicine or injection. Sudden loss of vision or hearing after an erection medicine also requires immediate medical advice. Do not take extra doses or wait for the next planned appointment to address these symptoms.

Persistent genital pain, sores, discharge or other changes deserve assessment even when they do not seem urgent. Tell the clinician if treatment is not helping or creates new problems. Sexual health can change across life; respectful communication and access to care remain useful at every age, whether or not sexual activity is a priority.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Consent and clinical care address different parts of sexual wellbeing. Respect for a boundary is unconditional, while symptoms such as persistent erection difficulties benefit from an individual assessment.

Treatments include lifestyle and psychological support, medicines, devices and selected procedures. Their risks differ; testosterone additionally requires a confirmed deficiency and attention to fertility.

How BeMama can help

Keep questions and a medicine list for a private health appointment if that is helpful. An app cannot determine the cause of an erection problem or replace consent between people.

When to seek help

An erection lasting more than four hours needs emergency care. Never combine PDE5 erection medicines with nitrates or poppers; seek immediate advice for sudden vision or hearing changes.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A refusal is not an invitation to persuade.
  • There is no required sexual performance or frequency.
  • Masturbation concerns depend on symptoms and daily impact, not an invented quota.
  • Repeated erection problems deserve assessment.
  • Medicine, hormone, device and surgical options have different precautions.

Frequently asked questions

Should I ask differently after my partner says no?

Accept the answer. Communication should clarify preferences and boundaries, not find a way around a refusal.

Does someone need a special word to stop an activity?

No. Any request to stop or indication of uncertainty is enough to pause and check.

Does masturbation automatically weaken erections?

No. It does not ordinarily cause erectile dysfunction, although rough handling can cause soreness or injury.

How often is too often?

There is no universal number. Consider pain, loss of control, distress and interference with everyday responsibilities.

Are erection problems always a sign of low attraction?

No. Physical health, medicines, fatigue, stress and other factors can contribute.

Can I stop a medicine if it seems to affect erections?

Discuss it with the prescriber first. A supervised change may be possible; stopping independently can be unsafe.

Can I take sildenafil with a nitrate for chest pain?

Do not combine them. Tell the prescriber about nitrates and all other medicines or recreational substances.

Will testosterone improve my fertility?

Not necessarily; testosterone treatment can suppress sperm production. Discuss current or future pregnancy plans before starting it.

Is an external vacuum pump the same as an implant?

No. A vacuum device is used outside the body; a prosthesis requires surgery and has different risks and long-term considerations.

What if an erection lasts longer than four hours?

Seek emergency assessment. Do not wait for it to settle or take another dose of an erection medicine.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
